periods.activity_title: Meet the Story: Read-Aloud and First Look

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the narrative by asking students what they know about parrots as pets, drawing on their own experiences to warm up to the story's world.

Teacher reads the full narrative aloud from Textbook pp. 41–52 with expression, pausing briefly at key moments — the parrot's plea for freedom, the merchant's journey, and the dramatic escape — so students absorb the plot arc.

Teacher re-reads pp. 41–52 paragraph by paragraph as a shared reading, inviting students to follow in their books and volunteer to read short passages aloud, building fluency and checking comprehension.
Brief whole-class oral recall: teacher asks 'What happened at the end?' and 'Were you surprised?' to anchor the plot in students' minds before moving to closer reading.

periods.teacher_notes: The story's twist — the wild parrot's coded message — can confuse first-time readers; re-read the escape scene slowly and allow students to voice confusion before clarifying. The merchant's refusal of the parrot's freedom request is emotionally charged, and students may have strong reactions worth briefly validating.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.45): answer five comprehension questions about the narrative.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads pp. 41–44 aloud at a brisk pace as a warm-up, reminding students of the merchant's relationship with the parrot and the parrot's longing, setting up the comprehension questions purposefully.

Let us Think A (p.45): teacher poses questions 1 and 2 — why the merchant kept a golden cage, and what made the parrot a favourite — students discuss in pairs and share responses; teacher builds a brief class answer together.

Let us Think A (p.45): teacher poses questions 3, 4, and 5 — the parrot's coded message, the reaction in the jungle, and the escape plan — students locate evidence in the text and frame oral answers before writing two sentences per question.
Whole-class review: teacher asks two students to share their written answers aloud, inviting peers to agree, disagree, or add detail, and the teacher clarifies the coded-message plot point firmly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate question 4 (the wild parrot falling from the tree) with question 5 (the pet parrot's ruse); a quick side-by-side re-read of pp. 48–50 clears this up. Written answers need only one or two sentences — the emphasis is on evidence from the text, not length.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.48): listen to bird sanctuary paragraph and answer oral questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students what they know about bird sanctuaries, accepting a few short answers to activate background knowledge and help students tune in to the listening passage.

Let us Listen (p.48): teacher reads the bird sanctuary paragraph aloud clearly and at a measured pace three times — first for gist, second for detail, third with a one-beat pause after each sentence so students can absorb key facts.

Let us Listen (p.48): teacher poses oral questions — how many bird sanctuaries in India, which is the oldest and where, which is the largest and where — students answer by raising hands and speaking in complete sentences; teacher confirms correct facts.
Quick pair-share: each student tells a partner one new fact they learned from the passage in their own words, and the teacher listens in, choosing two pairs to share with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage need three repetitions of a listening passage to retain factual details; do not skip any reading. The passage mentions Vedanthangal (Tamil Nadu) and Bharatpur (Rajasthan) — write these names on the board so spelling unfamiliarity does not block comprehension.

periods.activity_title: Sound Pairs and Picture Talk: Speaking Activities

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A (p.48–49): repeat 'ai' and 'oi' word pairs attending to vowel sounds.
Let us Speak B (p.49): look at caged and free bird pictures and share which you would prefer and why.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.45): discuss at home — which parrot was truly wise and why — and be ready to share one reason in class.

time_bands.activity: Let us Speak A (pp.48–49): teacher says each 'ai'/'oi' word pair (tail–toil, bail–boil, ail–oil, fail–foil, cane–coin, sail–soil) aloud, class repeats in chorus; then pairs take turns saying one column each, listening for the vowel shift.

Teacher picks four word pairs from Let us Speak A at random and asks individual students to say both words clearly, giving a quick thumbs-up or gentle correction on the vowel sound after each response.

Let us Speak B (p.49): teacher points to the two pictures — caged parrot and free parrot — and each student has a brief turn (sentence or two) saying which bird they would rather be and giving one reason; teacher thanks each speaker and echoes a notable reason back to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'ai' and 'oi' contrast is the phonics focus here; students who conflate the two vowels benefit from exaggerated mouth-shape modelling by the teacher. For Let us Speak B, accept any reasoned preference — there is no correct answer — and value students who connect their choice to the story's theme of freedom.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.46): fill in paragraph blanks with phrasal verbs from the box.
Let us Learn B (p.46): complete sentences using correct collective nouns from the word bank.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes three phrasal verbs from the box (stepped out, came across, look after) on the board, asks students to predict their meaning from context before defining, linking each to situations a Grade V student would recognise.

Let us Learn A (p.46): teacher reads the winter-morning paragraph aloud with blanks said as 'blank'; students suggest words from the box for each blank, justifying their choice, and the teacher confirms or redirects before students write answers in books.

Teacher introduces collective nouns briefly — 'a group word for many of the same thing' — writes 'a flight of parrots' on the board (the given example from Let us Learn B), and elicits what 'flight' signals about parrots to activate interest.

Let us Learn B (p.46): students work individually to fill sentences 2–7 with the correct collective noun; teacher circulates and after five minutes invites students to call out answers sentence by sentence while peers check their own work.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'went away' and 'came across' in Let us Learn A because both involve movement; ask them to read the sentence before and after the blank to decide direction of action. The collective noun 'army of ants' often surprises students — use it as a moment to discuss why language uses unexpected words for groups.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (pp.47–48): form present perfect tense sentences using has/have + past participle.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the two model sentences from Let us Learn C on the board — 'I have come from Jalandhar' and 'Rita has read all the poems by Sarojini Naidu' — and asks students what both sentences have in common, guiding them to notice has/have + verb form.

Teacher explains the present perfect rule (Subject + has/have + past participle + Object) with three quick board examples using familiar verbs (eat → has eaten, write → have written, visit → has visited), and students chorally say each completed sentence.

Let us Learn C (pp.47–48): teacher reads each sentence stem aloud with the verb in brackets; students decide has or have, form the past participle, and write the answer; teacher pauses at sentence (d) — which contains two blanks — to model both parts on the board.

Rapid oral check: teacher asks five students to read one completed sentence each aloud, and the class signals thumbs-up or thumbs-down for agreement, with teacher confirming and noting any irregular past participle that caused difficulty.

periods.teacher_notes: The irregular past participle of 'buy' (bought) and 'draw' (drawn) are the most common errors in Let us Learn C — write these on the board as anchor points before students begin the exercise. Sentence (d) has two subjects and two blanks; ask students to treat each clause separately rather than as one long sentence.

periods.activity_title: Continue the Story: The Parrot After Freedom

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.49–50): imagine and write the parrot's story after escaping the golden cage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the final lines of the narrative (pp. 51–52) where the parrot flies away, then tells students they are now the author who decides what happens next; teacher invites two or three brief oral ideas from the class to generate possibilities without fixing a single answer.

Modelled writing: teacher thinks aloud and writes the opening two sentences of the continuation on the board — 'After escaping from the golden cage, the parrot decided to fly deep into the jungle. It remembered every tree and every sound from its life before the cage.' — explaining each choice of detail and verb.

Let us Write (pp.49–50): students independently write their own continuation (four to six sentences) starting from the prompt given in the textbook; teacher circulates, reads over shoulders, asks guiding questions ('Where does the parrot go first? Who does it meet?') and gives brief oral nudges.

Two or three volunteers read their continuations aloud; the class listens and offers one word of appreciation for each — teacher closes by noting the variety of endings and affirming that imagination has no single right path.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who struggle to start can be reminded of the story's themes — freedom, wit, reunion — and encouraged to use one of these as their first idea. Writing and sharing happen in the same sitting; do not collect drafts for marking in a later sitting, as feedback given here is the formative element.

periods.activity_title: Bird Feeder Materials: Identify and Plan

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (pp.50–51): study six bird feeder pictures, identify materials used, and plan a feeder to make at home.

homework.task_brief: Let us Do (pp.50–51): with parental help, make a bird feeder at home using chosen material, fill it with seeds or grains, and place it outside.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook pp. 50–51 and gives students a quiet minute to look at all six bird feeder pictures; then asks 'What is a bird feeder for?' and takes two or three answers to establish purpose before focusing on materials.

Let us Do (pp.50–51): teacher points to each of the six feeders in turn — plastic bottle, coconut shell, bamboo log, ice-cream stick box, clay bowl, juice carton — students call out the material they see; teacher confirms and writes the six material names in a column on the board.

Students think independently about which material they would use for a home-made feeder and why, then share in pairs; four or five pairs report back to the class, and teacher notes the variety of choices on the board beside the material column.

Teacher explains the homework task — making and placing a feeder at home with parental help — students note the task brief in their homework diary; teacher emphasises that seeds, grains, or millets are suitable fills and that placement should be safe for birds.

periods.teacher_notes: The identification of the clay bowl and bamboo log feeders may be less familiar to urban students; give a moment to discuss what each material looks like before asking students to name it from the picture. The make-at-home component is genuine project work and requires parental involvement — alert students to discuss material choice with family tonight.

periods.activity_title: Bird Explorers: Facts About Two Birds

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore (p.52): choose two birds from the ten illustrated, research interesting facts, and share findings with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p.52 and names all ten birds in the illustration set — parrot, macaw, sparrow, crow, ostrich, seagull, pigeon, flamingo, weaver bird, tailor bird — students identify each in the picture; teacher asks which two birds students would most like to explore and tallies choices on the board.

Let us Explore (p.52): students choose their two birds from the ten and write three or four interesting facts per bird in their notebooks using any prior knowledge, information from the textbook picture captions, or a classroom reference if available; teacher circulates and prompts with questions such as 'What does it eat?' and 'Where does it live?'

Pairs share findings: each student reads one fact about one of their chosen birds to a partner, then the pair selects their most interesting combined fact and reports it to the class; teacher records one striking fact per bird named on the board.

Teacher closes by connecting the bird exploration back to the story — 'The parrot in our story wanted to return to the jungle; now you know what a rich world of birds lives there' — inviting one student to name the bird from the ten they would most want to see in the wild and why.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may not know much about the weaver bird or tailor bird beyond the names; steer curious students toward these two as a stretch challenge. The closing connection to the narrative theme of freedom and the natural world gives this final sitting its own coherent meaning.
materials: Classroom reference books or encyclopaedia (if available)

items.source_lo: Student infers character motivation and traces plot events using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Merchant's pet parrot, coded jungle message, and clever escape plan.
items.item_stem: Why did the parrot ask the merchant to carry greetings to its friends in the jungle rather than simply asking for freedom again?

options.label: A
options.text: The parrot had forgotten that it wanted to be free.

options.label: B
options.text: The parrot wanted to send a coded message to the wild parrots so they could help it escape.

options.label: C
options.text: The parrot was testing whether the merchant was honest.

options.label: D
options.text: The parrot wished to find out how far the jungle was from the village.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student has not followed the parrot's consistent longing for freedom throughout the story.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a misreading of the parrot's motive as moral testing rather than tactical planning.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows the student has not understood that the parrot's message was a strategy, not a geographical enquiry.

items.source_lo: Student infers character motivation and traces plot events using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Merchant's pet parrot, coded jungle message, and clever escape plan.
items.item_stem: Explain in your own words how the wild parrot's action in the jungle helped the caged parrot gain its freedom. Use details from the story in your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The wild parrot fell from the tree like a stone, as if dead, when it heard the merchant's message. This showed the caged parrot what to do: it also pretended to be dead, so the merchant lifted it out of the cage and placed it on the windowsill, from where it was able to fly away.

items.source_context: Bird sanctuaries in India: count, oldest (Vedanthangal, Tamil Nadu), largest (Bharatpur, Rajasthan).
items.item_stem: Listen carefully as your teacher reads the passage about bird sanctuaries in India. Then decide whether each statement below is true or false.

options.text: Bird sanctuaries are built to help endangered bird species survive.
The Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary in Rajasthan is the oldest bird sanctuary in India.
The Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary is located in Tamil Nadu.
There are more than 70 bird sanctuaries in India.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True; 2 — False (Bharatpur is the largest, not the oldest; Vedanthangal is the oldest); 3 — True; 4 — True.

items.source_context: Parrot escaping golden cage; story continuation from 'flew away' moment.
items.item_stem: Read the sentence below and choose the best way to continue the parrot's story after it escapes.

options.label: A
options.text: The parrot fell asleep on the rooftop and forgot about the jungle.

options.label: B
options.text: The parrot flew back into the golden cage because it missed its food.

options.label: C
options.text: The parrot soared into the jungle, called out to its friends, and breathed freely for the first time.

options.label: D
options.text: The parrot stayed on the windowsill and waited for the merchant to return.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student has not grasped the parrot's deep longing for freedom as the story's central theme.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a misunderstanding of why the parrot acted — waiting suggests passivity rather than the wit and purpose the story celebrates.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Shows the student has read the escape literally without connecting it to the narrative's resolution of the freedom theme.

expected_elements: Parrot moves to a place (jungle, tree, sky).
Parrot meets someone or notices something new.
Parrot's feeling of freedom is expressed.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any sentence where 'came across' clearly means 'found by chance' or 'met unexpectedly', for example: 'While walking to school, I came across a lost kitten near the gate.'

items.item_stem: Which bird from the ten shown on Textbook page 52 is the largest and cannot fly?

what_each_option_reveals.D: The sparrow is one of the smallest birds in the set — students who choose this may be guessing without recalling the bird's size.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Flamingos are large and distinctive but can fly; students who choose this may be thinking of size without considering the flight ability.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Pigeons are common and familiar but are capable fliers; this choice suggests the student has not connected the clue 'cannot fly' to the bird's identity.
